subject: biology
title: Factors affecting enzyme activity
key_idea: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change how fast an enzyme works. Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH. Too hot or too acidic or alkaline, and the active site changes shape, so the enzyme is denatured and stops working.

blocks.text: Temperature changes how fast the molecules move, and it can change the shape of the enzyme. Try the slider to see both effects.

items.meaning: The temperature or pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
The active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme cannot work.

diagram.alt: Change the temperature and watch the enzyme. The rate rises towards the optimum, then falls sharply as the active site changes shape.

items: The molecules have less kinetic energy and move more slowly.
There are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
The reaction is slow, but the enzyme is not denatured.
Higher temperature gives more kinetic energy and more collisions, so the rate rises up to the optimum.
Above the optimum the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits.
The enzyme is denatured and the rate falls to zero.
Rate rises with temperature up to the optimum, because of more collisions.
Too hot: the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
Too cold: the enzyme is slow, not denatured.

blocks.text: Each enzyme works best at one pH. Values above or below the optimum reduce the rate.

items: Enzymes are protein molecules with a 3D structure and an active site of a specific shape.
At pH values above or below the optimum, the shape of the active site changes in some molecules, so the rate decreases.
At extreme pH values the enzyme is denatured and the substrate can no longer fit.
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values. The protease in the stomach works in acid. Amylase works best at about pH 7 (neutral) and is denatured by the acid of the stomach.
Each enzyme has an optimum pH.
Extreme pH changes the shape of the active site and denatures the enzyme.
A denatured enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction, so the rate falls.

blocks.text: More substrate means more collisions with active sites, until every active site is in use.

items: Increasing the substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction, because there are more collisions with active sites.
More active sites are occupied and more enzyme-substrate complexes form.
Later the curve flattens. All the active sites are in use, so extra substrate makes no difference.
Increasing the enzyme concentration also increases the rate, because there are more active sites.
More substrate gives a faster rate, up to a limit.
The curve flattens when every active site is occupied.
More enzyme means more active sites and a faster rate.

blocks.text: Rate tells you how fast a reaction goes. You often work it out from the time taken or the amount of product.

blocks.label: Rate from the time taken
where: time taken for the reaction, in s

blocks.label: Rate from the amount
where: amount of substrate digested or product made, for example in g or cm³
time, for example in minutes or s

items.text: A potato disc rises in 75 seconds in 25% hydrogen peroxide.
To 3 decimal places the rate is 0.013 s⁻¹.

diagram.alt: Practise calculating a rate of reaction from the time taken.
diagram.question: A potato disc takes **{t} seconds** to rise in hydrogen peroxide solution. Calculate the rate of reaction in s⁻¹, using rate = 1 ÷ time. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

items: A shorter time means a faster rate.
Give the answer to the number of decimal places or significant figures the question asks for.

checks.q: Explain why an enzyme works slowly at 5 °C.
checks.a: The enzyme and substrate molecules have low kinetic energy, so there are fewer collisions and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.

checks.q: What happens to an enzyme at a very high temperature or an extreme pH?
checks.a: It is denatured. The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate can no longer fit.

checks.q: At pH 4, trypsin digested 1.5 g of mashed food in 2 minutes. At pH 1 it took 42 minutes to digest 1.5 g. Calculate the rate of digestion at pH 1 to 1 significant figure.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on amylase breaking down starch. Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present and is yellow-brown when there is no starch.

The table shows the time taken for the iodine solution to become yellow-brown.

5 °C: did not become yellow-brown
20 °C: 5 minutes
35 °C: 2 minutes
50 °C: 7 minutes
65 °C: 14 minutes
80 °C: did not become yellow-brown

Explain the results at 5 °C and at 80 °C.
answer_points: The iodine did not become yellow-brown because the starch was still present, or had not been broken down.
At 5 °C the amylase and starch molecules have low (kinetic) energy.
Therefore there are fewer enzyme-substrate collisions (allow: fewer enzyme-substrate complexes formed).
At 80 °C the amylase has been denatured (allow: the shape of the amylase or active site changes).
So the starch can no longer fit (allow: the bonds holding the amylase in its 3D shape have broken).
worked_example.tip: Treat the two temperatures separately. Low energy and fewer collisions for 5 °C. Denatured and the starch no longer fits for 80 °C. "Killed" is not accepted.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the effect of pH on the enzyme trypsin digesting mashed food.

At pH 4, the trypsin digested 1.5 g of mashed food at a rate of 0.8 g per minute. At pH 1, it took 42 minutes to digest the 1.5 g of mashed food.

Calculate the rate of digestion at pH 1.

Give your answer to one significant figure.
answer_points: Substitution: 1.5 ÷ 42 = 0.0357.
Evaluation: 0.04 g per minute (any correctly rounded value, for example 0.036, is accepted).
worked_example.tip: One mark for the substitution and one mark for the evaluation to one significant figure.

worked_example.question:
A student makes pineapple jelly using two different methods. Both methods use a protein called gelatin which causes the jelly to set.

Tinned pineapple is fresh pineapple which has been treated with heat.

Method 1: Fresh pineapple is added to the gelatin. It is left for 2 hours. The jelly does not set.
Method 2: Tinned pineapple is added to the gelatin. It is left for 2 hours. The jelly sets.

Pineapple contains an enzyme called bromelain. Bromelain digests proteins.

Explain why the jelly made with fresh pineapple does not set but the jelly made with tinned pineapple does set.

Use your knowledge of enzymes.
answer_points: Method 1: the bromelain (enzyme) breaks down the gelatin (protein), so the jelly cannot set.
Method 2: the bromelain (enzyme) has been denatured.
The active site of the enzyme changes shape, or the gelatin (protein) no longer fits into the active site.
The gelatin (protein) has not been broken down, so the jelly can set.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each of the four points. Heat denatures the enzyme. Do not say that the heat killed it.

worked_example.question:
Amylase is an enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of starch to form reducing sugars.
Plan an investigation to determine the effect of temperature on the rate of breakdown of starch by amylase.
answer_points: Independent variable: at least two temperatures.
Dependent variable: the time taken for a positive result for reducing sugar, or a negative result for starch.
Method: a way of maintaining each temperature, such as a water bath.
Method: use the iodine test or Benedict's test, taking samples at intervals.
Keep two things constant, such as the concentration and volume of starch, the concentration and volume of amylase, or the pH.
Repeat at least twice.
Give a relevant safety precaution.
worked_example.tip: Six marks are given across these points.

blocks.text: A temperature investigation changes one thing, the temperature, and measures how fast the enzyme works.

items.text: Put tubes of starch solution and amylase solution in water baths at different temperatures, such as 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C.
Add the amylase to the starch at each temperature and start a timer.
Take samples at intervals and add iodine. Record the time when the starch has gone and the iodine stays orange-brown.
Use the same volume and concentration of starch and amylase, and the same pH, at every temperature.
Repeat each temperature and find the mean time.

items: The shortest time shows the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest.
The temperature with the shortest time is close to the optimum.
Wear eye protection and take care with hot water.

worked_example.question:
Lipase digests lipid into fatty acids and glycerol. The fatty acids change the pH of the solution.
A student uses this method to investigate the effect of temperature on the activity of lipase.
Step 1 label a test tube with the temperature (20 °C)
Step 2 add 5 drops of phenolphthalein indicator to the test tube
Step 3 add 5 cm³ of milk to the test tube
Step 4 add 7 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution to the test tube (the contents of the test tube will now be pink)
Step 5 place a thermometer in the test tube
Step 6 place the test tube in a water bath at 20 °C for 5 minutes
Step 7 place a beaker containing lipase in the same water bath for 5 minutes
Step 8 replace the thermometer with a glass rod
Step 9 measure out 1 cm³ of lipase from the beaker in the water bath
Step 10 add the lipase to the test tube, stir the contents and record the time until the contents lose their pink colour
The student repeats this method for five more temperatures, 25 °C, 30 °C, 35 °C, 40 °C and 45 °C.
Explain why increasing temperature affects the time taken for the contents of the test tube to lose the pink colour.
answer_points: Increased kinetic energy, so molecules move faster.
More collisions, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form.
So the time to lose the pink colour decreases, up to the optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, bonds in the active site break and the enzyme is denatured.
The active site changes shape, so the enzyme and substrate can no longer fit.
worked_example.tip: Any four of these points score the marks.

blocks.text: In the practical, you change the temperature and time how long the reaction takes.

items.text: Warm the enzyme and its substrate separately in water baths at each temperature, such as 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C.
Mix them at that temperature and time the reaction. For example, time how long starch takes to disappear, or an indicator to change colour.
Keep the volume and concentration of enzyme and substrate, and the pH, the same each time.
Repeat each temperature and find the mean time.

items: A shorter time means a faster rate.
The temperature with the shortest time is closest to the optimum.
